title: Jugend ohne Gott
author: Ödön von Horváth
orthography: modernised to current German spelling (dass, muss, Schlussfolgerung, im Klaren, gestern Nachmittag, ...); wording unchanged; PDF line-break artefacts joined (wider sprechen → widersprechen etc.) and one typo fixed (m einem → in einem)
intro_en: Ödön von Horváth (1901–1938) wrote “Jugend ohne Gott” (Youth Without God) in 1937, in exile from Nazi Germany; the Nazis banned it straight away. A 34-year-old teacher in an unnamed fascist country watches his pupils turn into cold, obedient young people who only repeat what the radio says – and he has to decide whether he has the courage to speak up. It reads almost like a thriller, the sentences are short and modern, and German students still read it in school because its questions about courage and going along with the crowd haven't aged.

25. März. Auf meinem Tische stehen Blumen. Lieblich. Ein Geschenk meiner braven Hausfrau, denn heute ist mein Geburtstag.
Aber ich brauche den Tisch und rücke die Blumen beiseite und auch den Brief meiner alten Eltern. Meine Mutter schrieb: „Zu Deinem vierunddreißigsten Geburtstage wünsche ich Dir, mein liebes Kind, das Allerbeste. Gott, der Allmächtige, gebe Dir Gesundheit, Glück und Zufriedenheit!“ Und mein Vater schrieb: „Zu Deinem vierunddreißigsten Geburtstage, mein lieber Sohn, wünsche ich Dir alles Gute. Gott, der Allmächtige, gebe Dir Glück, Zufriedenheit und Gesundheit!“
units.en: 25 March. There are flowers on my table. Lovely. A present from my good landlady, because today is my birthday. But I need the table, so I push the flowers aside, and the letter from my old parents too. My mother wrote: “On your thirty-fourth birthday I wish you, my dear child, all the very best. May God Almighty give you health, happiness and contentment!” And my father wrote: “On your thirty-fourth birthday, my dear son, I wish you all the best. May God Almighty give you happiness, contentment and health!”
units.explain_en: The novel starts with the chapter “Die Neger”. The narrator is a 34-year-old teacher who writes like a diary, in the present tense. “Tische” and “Geburtstage” have an old dative -e; today: “auf meinem Tisch”, “zum Geburtstag”. “Hausfrau” here means his landlady (he rents a room); today that's “die Vermieterin” – “Hausfrau” now means housewife. “Gott gebe Dir …” is a wish (“May God give you …”) – this form only survives in fixed phrases.

units.de:
Glück kann man immer brauchen, denke ich mir, und gesund bist du auch, gottlob! Ich klopfe auf Holz. Aber zufrieden? Nein, zufrieden bin ich eigentlich nicht. Doch das ist ja schließlich niemand. Ich setze mich an den Tisch, entkorke eine rote Tinte, mach mir dabei die Finger tintig und ärgere mich darüber. Man sollt endlich mal eine Tinte erfinden, mit der man sich unmöglich tintig machen kann!
Nein, zufrieden bin ich wahrlich nicht.
units.en: Happiness always comes in handy, I think to myself, and you're healthy too, thank God! I knock on wood. But content? No, actually I'm not content. But then again, nobody is. I sit down at the table, uncork a bottle of red ink, get ink on my fingers doing it and get annoyed. Someone really ought to invent an ink you can't possibly get on your fingers! No, I am truly not content.
units.explain_en: He talks to himself as “du” – a habit through the whole book. “das Glück” means both luck and happiness. “auf Holz klopfen” = knock on wood, just like in English. “gottlob” is old; today: “Gott sei Dank”. “sich ärgern (über)” = to get annoyed (about) – very common. “Man sollt” = “Man sollte” (one should). “wahrlich” sounds biblical; today: “wirklich”.

units.de: Denk nicht so dumm, herrsch ich mich an. Du hast doch eine sichere Stellung mit Pensionsberechtigung, und das ist in der heutigen Zeit, wo niemand weiß, ob sich morgen die Erde noch drehen wird, allerhand! Wie viele würden sich sämtliche Finger ablecken, wenn sie an deiner Stelle wären?! Wie gering ist doch der Prozentsatz der Lehramtskandidaten, die wirklich Lehrer werden können!
units.en: Don't think such stupid things, I snap at myself. You've got a secure position with a pension, and in times like these, when no one knows whether the earth will still be turning tomorrow, that's quite something! How many people would lick every one of their fingers to be in your place?! How tiny the percentage of trainee teachers who actually get to be teachers is!
units.explain_en: In the 1930s many people were unemployed and war was in the air – so a safe job meant a lot. “sich anherrschen” = to snap at yourself. “allerhand” (quite something) is a bit old; today: “ganz schön viel”. “sich die Finger ablecken” comes from “sich alle zehn Finger nach etwas lecken” = to give anything for something. “die Stellung” is older; today: “die Stelle” or “der Job”. “an deiner Stelle” = in your place / if I were you – very useful.

units.de: Danke Gott, dass du zum Lehrkörper eines Städtischen Gymnasiums gehörst und dass du also ohne große wirtschaftliche Sorgen alt und blöd werden darfst! Du kannst doch auch hundert Jahre alt werden, vielleicht wirst du sogar mal der älteste Einwohner des Vaterlandes! Dann kommst du an deinem Geburtstag in die Illustrierte, und darunter wird stehen: „Er ist noch bei regem Geiste.“ Und das alles mit Pension! Bedenk und versündig dich nicht!
units.en: Thank God that you're on the teaching staff of a municipal grammar school, which means you can grow old and stupid without any big money worries! You might even live to be a hundred, maybe you'll even become the oldest inhabitant of the fatherland one day! Then on your birthday you'll be in the magazine, and underneath it'll say: “He is still mentally alert.” And all that with a pension! Think about it and don't sin by complaining!
units.explain_en: This is irony – he makes fun of his own safe life. “das Gymnasium” is the academic secondary school, NOT a gym (gym = die Turnhalle or das Fitnessstudio). “das Vaterland” was a favourite word of nationalist propaganda. “die Illustrierte” is an older word for a magazine; today: “die Zeitschrift”. “bei regem Geiste” is old; today: “geistig fit”. “sich versündigen” (to sin) sounds very old-fashioned.

units.de:
Ich versündige mich nicht und beginne zu arbeiten. Sechsundzwanzig blaue Hefte liegen neben mir, sechsundzwanzig Buben, so um das vierzehnte Jahr herum, hatten gestern in der Geographiestunde einen Aufsatz zu schreiben, ich unterrichte nämlich Geschichte und Geographie.
Draußen scheint noch die Sonne, fein muss es sein im Park! Doch Beruf ist Pflicht, ich korrigiere die Hefte und schreibe in mein Büchlein hinein, wer etwas taugt oder nicht.
units.en: I don't sin and I start working. Twenty-six blue exercise books lie beside me: twenty-six boys, all around fourteen, had to write an essay in geography class yesterday – I teach history and geography, you see. Outside the sun is still shining, it must be lovely in the park! But work is duty, so I correct the exercise books and write in my little notebook who's any good and who isn't.
units.explain_en: “das Heft” is still the normal word for a school exercise book. “die Buben” is southern German/Austrian for boys (in the north: “die Jungen” or “die Jungs”). “hatten … zu schreiben” = had to write (haben + zu + infinitive). “fein” is an older way of saying “schön”. “taugen” = to be any good; today you'd say “gut sein” or “etwas draufhaben”. “das Büchlein” is a little book (-lein, like -chen, makes things small).

Das von der Aufsichtsbehörde vorgeschriebene Thema der Aufsätze lautet: „Warum müssen wir Kolonien haben?“ Ja, warum? Nun, lasset uns hören!
Der erste Schüler beginnt mit einem B: er heißt Bauer, mit dem Vornamen Franz. In dieser Klasse gibt's keinen, der mit A beginnt, dafür haben wir aber gleich fünf mit B. Eine Seltenheit, so viele B's bei insgesamt sechsundzwanzig Schülern! Aber zwei B's sind Zwillinge, daher das Ungewöhnliche.
units.en: The essay topic prescribed by the school authorities is: “Why must we have colonies?” Yes, why? Well, let us hear! The first pupil begins with a B: his name is Bauer, first name Franz. In this class there's no one beginning with A, but to make up for it we have five with B straight away. A rarity, so many B's out of twenty-six pupils altogether! But two of the B's are twins, hence the unusual number.
units.explain_en: Background: Germany lost its colonies after World War I, and the Nazi government wanted them back – so schools had to set this topic. “lasset uns hören” is an old, Bible-style command; today: “hören wir mal”. “der Vorname” = first name. “dafür” here means “to make up for it”. Notice that the pupils are called by letters – they will become faceless in this book.

Well, Franz Bauer, why do we need colonies?
units.explain_en: He counts letters for no reason – a way of putting off a job he doesn't want to do. “überfliegen” = to skim (literally: to fly over). “feststellen” = to find out, to notice – very common (Ich habe festgestellt, dass …). “je zwei” = two each. “während” here means “while/whereas”. The letters matter: later the boys are just called N, T, Z …

units.de: „Wir brauchen die Kolonien“, schreibt er, „weil wir zahlreiche Rohstoffe benötigen, denn ohne Rohstoffe könnten wir unsere hochstehende Industrie nicht ihrem innersten Wesen und Werte nach beschäftigen, was zur unleidlichen Folge hätte, dass der heimische Arbeitsmann wieder arbeitslos werden würde.“ Sehr richtig, lieber Bauer! „Es dreht sich zwar nicht um die Arbeiter“ – sondern, Bauer? –, „es dreht sich vielmehr um das Volksganze, denn auch der Arbeiter gehört letzten Endes zum Volk.“
units.en: “We need the colonies,” he writes, “because we require numerous raw materials, for without raw materials we could not occupy our advanced industry according to its innermost nature and value, which would have the intolerable consequence that the working man at home would become unemployed again.” Quite right, dear Bauer! “It is not really about the workers” – but about what, Bauer? – “it is rather about the people as a whole, for the worker too ultimately belongs to the people.”
units.explain_en: The boy copies pompous propaganda phrases he doesn't really understand, and Horváth makes fun of them. “der Rohstoff” = raw material. “unleidlich” is old; today: “unerträglich”. “Es dreht sich um …” = it's about …; today people usually say “Es geht um …”. “das Volksganze” is typical Nazi-era jargon. “letzten Endes” (in the end, ultimately) is still normal.

units.de:
Das ist ohne Zweifel letzten Endes eine großartige Entdeckung, geht es mir durch den Sinn, und plötzlich fällt es mir wieder auf, wie häufig in unserer Zeit uralte Weisheiten als erstmalig formulierte Schlagworte serviert werden. Oder war das immer schon so? Ich weiß es nicht.
Jetzt weiß ich nur, dass ich wieder mal sechsundzwanzig Aufsätze durchlesen muss, Aufsätze, die mit schiefen Voraussetzungen falsche Schlussfolgerungen ziehen.
units.en: That is without doubt, ultimately, a great discovery, it crosses my mind, and suddenly it strikes me again how often in our times ancient wisdom gets served up as slogans that were supposedly coined for the first time. Or has it always been like that? I don't know. All I know right now is that once again I have to read through twenty-six essays, essays that draw false conclusions from skewed premises.
units.explain_en: The “great discovery” is sarcastic: of course workers are part of the people. “auffallen” = to strike, to notice (Mir fällt auf, dass …). “das Schlagwort” = slogan. “die Voraussetzung” means premise or requirement – very useful (Deutsch ist eine Voraussetzung für den Job). “die Schlussfolgerung” = conclusion. “wieder mal” is casual for “wieder einmal” (once again).

units.de: Wie schön wärs, wenn sich „schief“ und „falsch“ aufheben würden, aber sie tuns nicht. Sie wandeln Arm in Arm daher und singen hohle Phrasen. Ich werde mich hüten, als städtischer Beamter, an diesem lieblichen Gesange auch nur die leiseste Kritik zu üben! Wenns auch wehtut, was vermag der Einzelne gegen alle? Er kann sich nur heimlich ärgern. Und ich will mich nicht mehr ärgern! Korrigier rasch, du willst noch ins Kino!
units.en: How nice it would be if “skewed” and “false” cancelled each other out, but they don't. They stroll along arm in arm, singing empty phrases. As a municipal civil servant, I'll take good care not to make even the slightest criticism of this lovely singing! Even if it hurts, what can one person do against everyone? He can only get annoyed in secret. And I don't want to get annoyed any more! Correct them quickly, you still want to go to the cinema!
units.explain_en: Here is the big theme of the book: he knows the essays are wrong but is too scared to say so. “wärs” and “tuns” are short for “wäre es” and “tun es”. “Ich werde mich hüten!” = I'll take good care not to / I wouldn't dream of it – still used. “vermögen” (to be able to) is old; today: “können”. “der Beamte” = civil servant (teachers in Germany often are). “Gesange” has an old dative -e.

Und ich will schon mit roter Tinte an den Rand schreiben: „Sinnlose Verallgemeinerung!“ – da stocke ich. Aufgepasst, habe ich denn diesen Satz über die Neger in letzter Zeit nicht schon mal gehört? Wo denn nur? Richtig: er tönte aus dem Lautsprecher im Restaurant und verdarb mir fast den Appetit.
units.en: What's N writing here? “All Negroes are deceitful, cowardly and lazy.” – How stupid! Right, I'll cross that out! And I'm about to write in red ink in the margin: “Pointless generalisation!” – when I stop short. Careful, haven't I heard this sentence about the Negroes somewhere recently? But where? That's it: it came out of the loudspeaker in the restaurant and almost spoiled my appetite.
units.explain_en: Important: “Neger” is a racist slur today – never use it. Say “Schwarze” or “Schwarze Menschen”. Horváth uses it on purpose to show the racism of the 1930s. The sentence comes from state radio – so the teacher is afraid to cross it out. “durchstreichen” = to cross out. “der Rand” = the margin (or edge). “stocken” = to stop short, falter. “verderben” = to spoil (Das verdirbt mir den Appetit).

units.de: Ich lasse den Satz also stehen, denn was einer im Radio redet, darf kein Lehrer im Schulheft streichen. Und während ich weiterlese, höre ich immer das Radio: es lispelt, es heult, es bellt, es girrt, es droht – und die Zeitungen drucken es nach, und die Kindlein, sie schreiben es ab.
units.en: So I leave the sentence as it is, because no teacher may cross out in an exercise book what someone says on the radio. And as I read on, I keep hearing the radio: it lisps, it howls, it barks, it coos, it threatens – and the newspapers print it too, and the little children, they copy it down.

units.de: Nun hab ich den Buchstaben T verlassen, und schon kommt Z. Wo bleibt W? Habe ich das Heft verlegt? Nein, der W war ja gestern krank – er hatte sich am Sonntag im Stadion eine Lungenentzündung geholt, stimmt, der Vater hats mir ja schriftlich korrekt mitgeteilt. Armer W! Warum gehst du auch ins Stadion, wenns eisig in Strömen regnet?
units.en: Now I've left the letter T behind, and already here comes Z. Where's W? Have I mislaid the exercise book? No, W was off sick yesterday – he caught pneumonia at the stadium on Sunday, that's right, his father let me know properly in writing. Poor W! Why do you go to the stadium anyway when it's pouring with icy rain?

Diese Frage könntest du eigentlich auch an dich selbst stellen, fällt es mir ein, denn du warst ja am Sonntag ebenfalls im Stadion und harrtest treu bis zum Schlusspfiff aus, obwohl der Fußball, den die beiden Mannschaften boten, keineswegs hochklassig war. Ja, das Spiel war sogar ausgesprochen langweilig – also: warum bliebst du? Und mit dir dreißigtausend zahlende Zuschauer?
Warum?
units.en: Actually you could ask yourself the same question, it occurs to me, because you were at the stadium on Sunday too and stuck it out loyally until the final whistle, even though the football the two teams played was by no means top class. In fact the match was downright boring – so: why did you stay? And thirty thousand paying spectators with you? Why?

Note the question: why do people stay at a boring game? The answer comes next.

Wenn der Rechtsaußen den linken Half überspielt und zentert, wenn der Mittelstürmer den Ball in den leeren Raum vorlegt und der Tormann sich wirft, wenn der Halblinke seine Verteidigung entlastet und ein Flügelspiel forciert, wenn der Verteidiger auf der Torlinie rettet, wenn einer unfair rempelt oder eine ritterliche Geste macht, wenn der Schiedsrichter gut ist oder schwach, parteiisch oder parteilos, dann existiert für den Zuschauer nichts auf der Welt außer dem Fußball, ob die Sonne scheint, obs regnet oder schneit. Dann hat er alles vergessen.
Was „alles“?
Ich muss lächeln: die Neger, wahrscheinlich –
units.en: When the right winger beats the left half and crosses, when the centre forward plays the ball into space and the goalkeeper dives, when the inside left takes pressure off his defence and forces play down the wing, when the defender clears off the goal line, when someone barges unfairly or makes a sporting gesture, when the referee is good or weak, biased or fair, then nothing in the world exists for the spectator except football, whether the sun shines, whether it rains or snows. Then he has forgotten everything. What “everything”? I have to smile: the Negroes, probably –
units.explain_en: One huge sentence of “wenn” clauses – each with the verb at the end. Some football words are from the 1930s: “zentern” → today “flanken”; “der Tormann” (Austrian) → “der Torwart”; “der Half” and “der Halblinke” are positions that don't exist any more. The point: football makes people forget injustice. “obs” = “ob es”. Important: “Neger” is a racist slur today – never use it. Say “Schwarze” or “Schwarze Menschen”. Horváth uses it on purpose to show the racism of the 1930s.

Als ich am nächsten Morgen in das Gymnasium kam und die Treppe zum Lehrerzimmer emporstieg, hörte ich auf dem zweiten Stock einen wüsten Lärm. Ich eilte empor und sah, dass fünf Jungen, und zwar E, G, R, H, T, einen verprügelten, nämlich den F.
„Was fällt euch denn ein?“ schrie ich sie an. „Wenn ihr schon glaubt, noch raufen zu müssen wie die Volksschüler, dann rauft doch gefälligst einer gegen einen, aber fünf gegen einen, also das ist eine Feigheit!“
units.en: When I came into the grammar school the next morning and went up the stairs to the staff room, I heard a terrible racket on the second floor. I hurried up and saw five boys, namely E, G, R, H and T, beating up another boy, namely F. “What do you think you're doing?” I shouted at them. “If you really think you still have to scrap like primary school kids, then at least fight one against one – but five against one, that's cowardly!”
units.explain_en: New chapter: “Es regnet” (It's raining). Now he writes in the past tense. “Was fällt euch denn ein?” = What do you think you're doing? / How dare you? – very common for telling someone off. “raufen” (to scrap) is southern; everywhere: “sich prügeln”. “die Volksschüler” is old/Austrian for primary school pupils (today: Grundschüler). “gefälligst” shows annoyance, like “kindly …”.

units.de: Sie sahen mich verständnislos an, auch der F, über den die fünf hergefallen waren. Sein Kragen war zerrissen. „Was hat er euch denn getan?“ fragte ich weiter, doch die Helden wollten nicht recht heraus mit der Sprache und auch der Verprügelte nicht. Erst allmählich brachte ich es heraus, dass der F den fünfen nichts angetan hatte, sondern im Gegenteil: die fünf hatten ihm seine Buttersemmel gestohlen, nicht, um sie zu essen, sondern nur, damit er keine hat. Sie haben die Semmel durch das Fenster auf den Hof geschmissen.
units.en: They looked at me blankly, even F, whom the five had attacked. His collar was torn. “What has he done to you, then?” I went on asking, but the heroes didn't really want to come out with it, and neither did the boy they'd beaten. Only gradually did I find out that F hadn't done anything to the five; on the contrary: the five had stolen his buttered roll, not to eat it, but only so that he wouldn't have one. They threw the roll out of the window into the yard.
units.explain_en: “die Semmel” is the southern German/Austrian word for a bread roll; in the north: “das Brötchen”. “schmeißen” is casual for “werfen” (to throw) – very common in speech. “im Gegenteil” = on the contrary. “allmählich” = gradually. “nicht recht heraus mit der Sprache wollen” = not want to come out with it. The cruelty is pointless – that's what shocks him.

Ich schaue hinab. Dort liegt sie auf dem grauen Stein. Es regnet noch immer, und die Semmel leuchtet hell herauf.
Und ich denke: vielleicht haben die fünf keine Semmeln, und es ärgert sie, dass der F eine hatte. Doch nein, sie hatten alle ihre Semmeln, und der G sogar zwei. Und ich frage nochmals: „Warum habt ihr das also getan?“ Sie wissen es selber nicht. Sie stehen vor mir und grinsen verlegen.
units.en: I look down. There it lies on the grey stone. It's still raining, and the roll shines brightly up at me. And I think: maybe the five don't have any rolls, and it annoys them that F had one. But no, they all had their rolls, and G even had two. And I ask again: “So why did you do it?” They don't know themselves. They stand in front of me grinning sheepishly.
units.explain_en: The switch back to the present tense makes the scene feel like it's happening right now. “hinab” and “herauf” are literary; in speech: “runter” and “rauf”. “nochmals” = again; today: “noch mal”. “selber” is the casual form of “selbst” (themselves). “verlegen grinsen” = to grin sheepishly.

Ja, der Mensch dürfte wohl böse sein, und das steht auch schon in der Bibel. Als es aufhörte zu regnen und die Wasser der Sündflut wieder wichen, sagte Gott: „Ich will hinfort nicht mehr die Erde strafen um der Menschen willen, denn das Trachten des menschlichen Herzens ist böse von Jugend auf.“
Hat Gott sein Versprechen gehalten? Ich weiß es noch nicht. Aber ich frage nun nicht mehr, warum sie die Semmel auf den Hof geworfen haben.
units.en: Yes, people may well be evil, and that's already in the Bible. When it stopped raining and the waters of the Flood went down, God said: “I will never again curse the earth because of man, for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth.” Has God kept his promise? I don't know yet. But I no longer ask why they threw the roll into the yard.
units.explain_en: God's words come from Genesis 8:21 – “Jugend” (youth) and “Gott” link to the book's title, “Jugend ohne Gott” (Youth Without God). “die Sündflut” is an old form; today: “die Sintflut”. “hinfort” is biblical for “from now on”. “um der Menschen willen” = for the sake of people. “ein Versprechen halten” = to keep a promise – very useful.

units.de: Ich erkundige mich nur, ob sie es noch nie gehört hätten, dass sich seit Urzeiten her, seit tausend und tausend Jahren, seit dem Beginn der menschlichen Gesittung, immer stärker und stärker ein ungeschriebenes Gesetz herausgebildet hat, ein männliches Gesetz: Wenn ihr schon rauft, dann raufe nur einer gegen einen! Bleibet immer ritterlich! Und ich wende mich wieder an die fünf und frage: „Schämt ihr euch denn nicht?“
units.en: I only ask them whether they've never heard that since the dawn of time, for thousands and thousands of years, since the beginning of human civilisation, an unwritten law has grown stronger and stronger, a manly law: If you have to fight, then only one against one! Always be chivalrous! And I turn back to the five and ask: “Aren't you ashamed of yourselves?”

„Schließt das Fenster“, sage ich, „sonst regnets noch herein!“

He's laughing at me. “Shut the window,” I say, “or the rain will get in!” They shut it. What kind of generation is this going to be? A tough one or just a brutal one? units.de: Von 10–11 hatte ich Geographie. In dieser Stunde musste ich die gestern korrigierte Schulaufgabe betreffs der kolonialen Frage drannehmen. Wie bereits erwähnt, hatte man gegen den Inhalt der Aufsätze vorschriftsgemäß nichts einzuwenden. Ich sprach also, während ich nun die Hefte an die Schüler verteilte, lediglich über Sprachgefühl, Orthographie und Formalitäten. So sagte ich dem einen B, er möge nicht immer über den linken Rand hinausschreiben, dem R, die Absätze müssten größer sein, dem Z, man schreibt Kolonien mit e und nicht Kolonihn mit h.
units.en: From 10 to 11 I had geography. In this lesson I had to go over the class essay on the colonial question that I'd corrected the day before. As I've already mentioned, according to the rules there was nothing to object to in the content of the essays. So while I handed the exercise books out to the pupils, I only talked about feel for language, spelling and formalities. So I told one of the B's not to keep writing over the left margin, R that his paragraphs had to be bigger, and Z that you write Kolonien with an e and not Kolonihn with an h.
units.explain_en: New chapter: “Die reichen Plebejer” (The Rich Plebeians). “betreffs” is office language for “about”; today: “zu” or “über”. “drannehmen” is casual for dealing with something in class (or calling on a pupil). “einwenden” = to object. The told-them-that parts use indirect speech: “er möge …”, “die Absätze müssten …”. “die Orthographie” is old; today: “die Rechtschreibung”.

Aber du darfst doch nicht schreiben, dass es auf die Neger nicht ankommt, ob sie nämlich leben könnten oder nicht. Auch die Neger sind doch Menschen.“
units.en: Only when I gave N his exercise book back couldn't I hold back: “You write,” I said, “that we whites stand above the Negroes culturally and in terms of civilisation, and that may well be true. But you really can't write that it doesn't matter whether the Negroes are able to live or not. The Negroes are human beings too, after all.”

units.de: Bereits am nächsten Tage erschien der Vater des N in meiner Sprechstunde, die ich wöchentlich einmal abhalten musste, um mit den Eltern in Kontakt zu kommen. units.de: Nun stand der Vater des N vor mir. Er hatte einen selbstsicheren Gang und sah mir aufrecht in die Augen. „Ich bin der Vater des Otto N.“ „Freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen, Herr N“, antwortete ich, verbeugte mich, wie es sich gehört, bot ihm Platz an, doch er setzte sich nicht. „Herr Lehrer“, begann er, „mein Hiersein hat den Grund in einer überaus ernsten Angelegenheit, die wohl noch schwerwiegende Folgen haben dürfte. Mein Sohn Otto teilte mir gestern Nachmittag in heller Empörung mit, dass Sie, Herr Lehrer, eine schier unerhörte Bemerkung fallen gelassen hätten –“ „Ich?“
units.en: Now N's father stood in front of me. He had a self-assured walk and looked me straight in the eye. “I am the father of Otto N.” “Pleased to meet you, Mr N,” I replied, bowed as is proper, and offered him a seat, but he didn't sit down. “Teacher,” he began, “my presence here is on account of an extremely serious matter, which may well have grave consequences. Yesterday afternoon my son Otto informed me in great indignation that you, Teacher, had let drop a quite outrageous remark –” “I?”

Das ist Sabotage am Vaterland! Oh, mir machen Sie nichts vor! Ich weiß es nur zu gut, auf welch heimlichen Wegen und mit welch perfiden Schlichen das Gift ihrer Humanitätsduselei unschuldige Kinderseelen zu unterhöhlen trachtet!“
Nun wurds mir aber zu bunt! „Erlauben Sie“, brauste ich auf, „das steht doch bereits in der Bibel, dass alle Menschen Menschen sind!“
units.en: “Excuse me, please,” he interrupted me sharply, “I am in no mood for jokes! You clearly don't yet realise what such a remark about the Negroes means?! It is sabotage against the fatherland! Oh, you can't fool me! I know only too well by what secret paths and with what perfidious tricks the poison of this humanitarian soppiness seeks to undermine innocent children's souls!” Now that was too much for me! “Excuse me,” I flared up, “it already says in the Bible that all people are human beings!”

Ein gewisser Bäckermeister N hat sich über Sie beschwert, Sie sollen da so Äußerungen fallen gelassen haben. – Nun, ich kenne das und weiß, wie solche Beschwerden zustande kommen, mir müssen Sie nichts erklären! Doch, lieber Kollege, ist es meine Pflicht, Sie darauf aufmerksam zu machen, dass sich derlei nicht wiederholt. Sie vergessen das geheime Rundschreiben 5679 u/33! Wir müssen von der Jugend alles fernhalten, was nur in irgendeiner Weise ihre zukünftigen militärischen Fähigkeiten beeinträchtigen könnte – das heißt: wir müssen sie moralisch zum Krieg erziehen. Punkt!“
units.en: The headmaster had sent for me. “Listen,” he said, “a letter has come from the education authority. A certain master baker N has complained about you – you're supposed to have let drop some remarks or other. Now, I know how it is, and I know how complaints like that come about; you don't have to explain anything to me! But, my dear colleague, it is my duty to point out to you that this sort of thing must not happen again. You are forgetting secret circular 5679 u/33! We must keep away from young people anything that could in any way harm their future military abilities – that means: we must educate them morally for war. Full stop!”

He's a handsome old man, I thought. “You are surprised,” he said suddenly, “that I'm blowing the war trumpet, and you are right to be surprised! You're thinking now: behold, what a man! Only a few years ago he was signing fiery messages of peace, and today? Today he's arming for battle!” “I know you're only doing it because you're forced to,” I said, trying to calm him down.

Er horchte auf, blieb vor mir stehen und sah mich aufmerksam an. „Junger Mann“, sagte er ernst, „merken Sie sich eines: es gibt keinen Zwang. Ich könnte ja dem Zeitgeist widersprechen und mich von einem Herrn Bäckermeister einsperren lassen, ich könnte ja hier gehen, aber ich will nicht gehen, jawohl, ich will nicht! Denn ich möchte die Altersgrenze erreichen, um die volle Pension beziehen zu können.“
Das ist ja recht fein, dachte ich.
units.en: He pricked up his ears, stopped in front of me and looked at me closely. “Young man,” he said seriously, “remember one thing: there is no such thing as being forced. I could, after all, contradict the spirit of the age and let some master baker have me locked up; I could leave this place – but I don't want to leave, yes indeed, I don't want to! Because I'd like to reach retirement age so that I can draw my full pension.” That's very nice indeed, I thought.
units.explain_en: The headmaster is honest in a cynical way: he goes along with the regime for the sake of his pension. ‘aufhorchen’ = to prick up one's ears. ‘sich etwas merken’ = to remember something (Merk dir das!). ‘der Zwang’ = compulsion. ‘der Zeitgeist’ (spirit of the age) is also used in English. ‘einsperren’ = to lock up. ‘Pension beziehen’ = to draw a pension; in Germany today ‘Pension’ is for civil servants, other people get ‘Rente’. ‘Das ist ja recht fein’ is ironic.

units.en: The headmaster says they live in a “plebeian world” – a world ruled by common people – and compares it to ancient Rome. When the teacher objects that it is really money that rules, the headmaster agrees and reminds him that in Rome there were also rich plebeians: they left the ordinary people and joined the old aristocracy to form a new ruling class. “Don't forget that again!” he says. The teacher understands: the people in power today are just such rich plebeians.

Als ich zur nächsten Stunde die Klasse, in der ich mir erlaubte, etwas über die Neger zu sagen, betrete, fühle ich sogleich, dass etwas nicht in Ordnung ist. Haben die Herren meinen Stuhl mit Tinte beschmiert? Nein. Warum schauen sie mich nur so schadenfroh an?
Da hebt einer die Hand. Was gibts? Er kommt zu mir, verbeugt sich leicht, überreicht mir einen Brief und setzt sich wieder.
Was soll das?
Ich erbreche den Brief, überfliege ihn, möchte hochfahren, beherrsche mich jedoch und tue, als würd ich ihn genau lesen. Ja, alle haben ihn unterschrieben, alle fünfundzwanzig, der W ist noch immer krank.
units.en: When, at the next lesson, I walk into the class where I took the liberty of saying something about the Negroes, I sense at once that something is wrong. Have the gentlemen smeared ink on my chair? No. So why are they looking at me with such malicious glee? Then one of them raises his hand. What is it? He comes up to me, bows slightly, hands me a letter and sits down again. What's this about? I open the letter, skim through it, want to jump up, but control myself and pretend to be reading it carefully. Yes, they've all signed it, all twenty-five – W is still ill.
units.explain_en: This chapter is called ‘Das Brot’ (bread = his living). Notice the switch to the present tense. ‘sich erlauben, etwas zu tun’ = to take the liberty of doing something. ‘schadenfroh’ = gloating (die Schadenfreude, a word English borrowed). ‘Was gibts?’ = What's up? ‘einen Brief erbrechen’ is old for ‘öffnen’ – today ‘erbrechen’ means to vomit! ‘sich beherrschen’ = to control oneself. Important: ‘Neger’ is a racist slur today – never use it; say ‘Schwarze’ or ‘Schwarze Menschen’.

„Wir wünschen nicht mehr“, steht in dem Brief, „von Ihnen unterrichtet zu werden, denn nach dem Vorgefallenen haben wir Endesunterzeichneten kein Vertrauen mehr zu Ihnen und bitten um eine andere Lehrkraft.“
Ich blicke die Endesunterzeichneten an, einen nach dem anderen. Sie schweigen und sehen mich nicht an. Ich unterdrücke meine Erregung und frage wie so nebenbei: „Wer hat das geschrieben?“

units.en: “We no longer wish,” it says in the letter, “to be taught by you, because after what has happened, we the undersigned no longer have any trust in you and ask for a different teacher.” I look at the undersigned, one after another. They are silent and don't look at me. I suppress my agitation and ask, as if in passing: “Who wrote this?” Nobody puts his hand up. “Don't be such cowards!” They don't move.

units.en: Then the teacher sees a boy secretly writing down every word he says – they are spying on him. The headmaster shouts at the class like a good actor, but nothing changes. Alone at home, the teacher decides he will not lose his job: from now on he will only tell them what the radio says. He feels that hate has spread like a plague and that he is infected too. That night he goes to the cinema and then to a cheap bar, gets very drunk and meets a former colleague everyone calls “Julius Caesar”. After a scandal and a prison sentence, Caesar now sells cheap goods from door to door and wears a tiny skull tie-pin with a light inside. Caesar lectures him about the generations and tells him about a boy who secretly read a banned book.

units.de:
„Sie glauben also, dass einzelne von denen heimlich lesen?“
„Ich weiß es. Bei jener Dame ist manchmal ein direktes Kränzchen, sie ist oft schon ganz außer sich. Die Buben lesen alles. Aber sie lesen nur, um spötteln zu können. Sie leben in einem Paradies der Dummheit, und ihr Ideal ist der Hohn. Es kommen kalte Zeiten, das Zeitalter der Fische.“
„Der Fische?“
„Ich bin zwar nur ein Amateurastrolog, aber die Erde dreht sich in das Zeichen der Fische hinein. Da wird die Seele des Menschen unbeweglich wie das Antlitz eines Fisches.“ –
units.en: “So you think some of them read in secret?” “I know it. That lady sometimes has a regular little circle at her place, and she's often quite beside herself. The boys read everything. But they only read so they can sneer. They live in a paradise of stupidity, and their ideal is mockery. Cold times are coming – the Age of the Fish.” “Of the Fish?” “I'm only an amateur astrologer, but the earth is turning into the sign of Pisces. Then the human soul will become as motionless as the face of a fish.”
units.explain_en: This is the key image of the novel: young people with ‘fish faces’ – cold, showing no feeling. Astrologers speak of the ‘Age of Pisces’ (Fische = fish and the star sign Pisces). ‘das Kränzchen’ = a small regular get-together (Kaffeekränzchen). ‘außer sich sein’ = to be beside oneself. ‘die Buben’ is southern German/Austrian for ‘die Jungen’. ‘spötteln’ = to make little mocking remarks; ‘der Hohn’ = scorn. ‘das Antlitz’ is poetic for ‘das Gesicht’.

units.en: The teacher wakes up in a stranger's flat and goes home at dawn. A small man is waiting for him: the father of W, the boy who was ill. W caught pneumonia at the football stadium and is dying. In his fever he keeps asking to see his hero, the famous goalkeeper of the national team. The teacher knows where the goalkeeper lives and goes to fetch him. The goalkeeper leaves his breakfast, takes a taxi with him and sits quietly by the bed of the smallest boy in the class. “When are you playing England?” W asks. “Tell me, tell me!”

units.de: Und der Tormann erzählte. Er sprach von berühmt gewordenen Siegen und unverdienten Niederlagen, von strengen Schiedsrichtern und korrupten Linienrichtern. Er stand auf, nahm zwei Stühle, markierte mit ihnen das Tor und demonstrierte, wie er einst zwei Elfer hintereinander abgewehrt hatte. Er zeigte seine Narbe auf der Stirne, die er sich in Lissabon bei einer tollkühnen Parade geholt hatte. Und er sprach von fernen Ländern, in denen er sein Heiligtum hütete, von Afrika, wo die Beduinen mit dem Gewehr im Publikum sitzen, und von der schönen Insel Malta, wo das Spielfeld leider aus Stein besteht –
units.en: And the goalkeeper told him. He talked about victories that had become famous and undeserved defeats, about strict referees and corrupt linesmen. He stood up, took two chairs, marked out the goal with them and showed how he had once saved two penalties in a row. He showed the scar on his forehead that he had got in Lisbon making a daring save. And he talked about faraway countries where he had guarded his sanctuary, about Africa, where the Bedouins sit in the crowd with rifles, and about the beautiful island of Malta, where the pitch is unfortunately made of stone –
units.explain_en: A gentle scene with lots of football vocabulary. ‘der Tormann’ is Austrian; in Germany ‘der Torwart’. ‘der Elfer’ = penalty (today: ‘der Elfmeter’). ‘abwehren’ = to save, fend off. ‘die Parade’ here is a goalkeeper's save. ‘der Schiedsrichter’ = referee, ‘der Linienrichter’ = linesman. ‘sein Heiligtum hüten’ – calling the goal a ‘sanctuary’ – is a joke. ‘die Stirne’ is old for ‘die Stirn’.

Und während der Tormann erzählte, schlief der kleine W ein. Mit einem seligen Lächeln, still und friedlich. – – –
Das Begräbnis fand an einem Mittwoch statt, nachmittags um halb zwei. Die Märzsonne schien, Ostern war nicht mehr weit.
 Wir standen um das offene Grab. Der Sarg lag schon drunten.
Der Direktor war anwesend mit fast allen Kollegen, nur der Physiker fehlte, ein Sonderling. Der Pfarrer hielt die Grabrede, die Eltern und einige Verwandte verharrten regungslos.
Und im Halbkreis uns gegenüber standen die Mitschüler des Verstorbenen, die ganze Klasse, alle fünfundzwanzig.
Neben dem Grab lagen die Blumen. Ein schöner Kranz trug auf einer gelb-grünen Schleife die Worte: „Letzte Grüße Dein Tormann.“
units.en: And while the goalkeeper was talking, little W fell asleep. With a blissful smile, quiet and peaceful. The funeral took place on a Wednesday, at half past one in the afternoon. The March sun was shining; Easter was not far off. We stood around the open grave. The coffin was already down below. The headmaster was there with almost all the teachers; only the physics teacher was missing, an odd character. The priest gave the graveside speech; the parents and a few relatives stood motionless. And in a semicircle opposite us stood the dead boy's classmates, the whole class, all twenty-five. The flowers lay next to the grave. On a yellow-and-green ribbon, a beautiful wreath bore the words: “Last greetings, your goalkeeper.”

units.en: During the priest's speech the teacher notices N among the boys. N's face shows nothing, but when he looks at the teacher, the teacher feels that N is his deadly enemy and wishes him dead. He decides not to show that he knows what N is thinking, and to keep his modest ideals to himself: other generations will come after N.

units.en: For some years now, the authorities have used the Easter holidays for “tent camps” – military training for schoolboys. The class travels by bus to a poor mountain village. The mayor shows the teacher a big sawmill that was closed down to make more profit, and the village teacher explains that half the villagers do badly paid work at home and a third of the children are underfed. The priest warns him that a class of girls is staying in a castle nearby. Up on a meadow, a retired sergeant (Feldwebel) and the boys put up the tents. Next to the flagpole stands a big crate full of rifles, and the targets are wooden soldiers in a foreign uniform. In the evening they sing soldiers' songs.

units.de:
Es wird Nacht.
Wir gehen schlafen. „Morgen beginnt der Ernst!“ meint der Feldwebel.
Er schläft mit mir im selben Zelt.
Ich entzünde noch mal meine Taschenlampe, um nach der Uhr zu sehen, und entdecke dabei auf der Zeltwand neben mir einen braunroten Fleck.
Was ist das?
Und ich denke, morgen beginnt der Ernst. Ja, der Ernst. In einer Kiste neben der Fahnenstange liegt der Krieg. Ja, der Krieg.
units.en: Night falls. We go to bed. “Tomorrow things get serious!” says the sergeant. He sleeps in the same tent as me. I switch on my torch once more to look at my watch, and as I do so I discover a reddish-brown stain on the tent wall beside me. What is that? And I think: tomorrow things get serious. Yes, serious. In a crate next to the flagpole lies war. Yes, war.
units.explain_en: ‘Der Ernst beginnt’ = things get serious (der Ernst = seriousness; ‘Das ist mein Ernst’ = I mean it). ‘die Taschenlampe’ = torch, flashlight. ‘nach der Uhr sehen’ = to check the time. ‘entdecken’ = to discover. ‘braunrot’ – colour compounds are easy in German: blaugrün, hellblau. The stain and the crate of rifles are warning signs of what is coming.

units.covers: Chapters 'Der totale Krieg' (end) to 'Auf der Suche nach den Idealen der Menschheit' (beginning)
units.en: Training begins. A class of girls marches past; their war game is to search for a pretend “missing pilot”. Out walking, the teacher sees three poor, barefoot children – two boys and an older girl – trick a blind old farmer's wife and steal a loaf of bread; the old woman falls. A farmer says a gang of children keeps stealing: “weeds that should be wiped out”. The sergeant sets up night guards. In the village, the priest takes the teacher down the street of the home workers, where pale children sit at dark windows painting dolls and do not greet the priest. In the priest's house the teacher sees a picture of the Crucifixion with a Roman captain. Over wine they argue: the priest says the Church sides with the rich because the rich always win.

units.de:
„Möglich“, antworte ich kurz und merke, dass ich aufgeregt bin. „Doch kommen wir wieder auf jene Kinder in den Fenstern zurück! Sie sagten, als wir durch die Gasse gingen: ‚Sie grüßen mich nicht, sie sind verhetzt.‘ Sie sind doch ein gescheiter Mensch, Sie müssen es doch wissen, dass jene Kinder nicht verhetzt sind, sondern dass sie nichts zum Fressen haben!“
Er sieht mich groß an.
„Ich meinte, sie seien verhetzt“, sagte er langsam, „weil sie nicht mehr an Gott glauben.“
„Wie können Sie das von ihnen verlangen!“
units.en: “Possibly,” I answer shortly, and notice that I'm worked up. “But let's come back to those children in the windows! When we were walking down the lane you said: ‘They don't greet me, they've been stirred up.’ You're an intelligent man, surely you must know that those children haven't been stirred up – they simply have nothing to eat!” He looks at me wide-eyed. “I meant they had been stirred up,” he said slowly, “because they no longer believe in God.” “How can you expect that of them!”
units.explain_en: ‘aufgeregt’ = worked up, excited. ‘verhetzt’ = stirred up, turned against someone (die Hetze = hate campaign). ‘gescheit’ is southern German/Austrian for ‘klug’. ‘nichts zum Fressen haben’ – ‘fressen’ is how animals eat; used for people it is rude and shows his anger. ‘jemanden groß ansehen’ = to look at someone in surprise. ‘sie seien’ is Konjunktiv I for reported speech. ‘verlangen’ = to demand, expect.

units.de:
„Gott geht durch alle Gassen.“
„Wie kann Gott durch jene Gasse gehen, die Kinder sehen und ihnen nicht helfen?“
Er schweigt. Er trinkt bedächtig seinen Wein aus. Dann sieht er mich wieder groß an: „Gott ist das Schrecklichste auf der Welt.“
Ich starre ihn an. Hatte ich richtig gehört? Das Schrecklichste?!
Er erhebt sich, tritt an das Fenster und schaut auf den Friedhof hinaus. „Er straft“, höre ich seine Stimme. Was ist das für ein erbärmlicher Gott, denke ich mir, der die armen Kinder straft!
Jetzt geht der Pfarrer auf und ab.
units.en: “God walks through every lane.” “How can God walk through that lane, see the children and not help them?” He is silent. He slowly finishes his wine. Then he looks at me wide-eyed again: “God is the most terrible thing in the world.” I stare at him. Had I heard right? The most terrible thing?! He gets up, goes to the window and looks out at the graveyard. “He punishes,” I hear his voice say. What a pitiful God that is, I think to myself, who punishes poor children! Now the priest walks up and down.
units.explain_en: ‘Gott ist das Schrecklichste auf der Welt’ is one of the most important sentences in the book – remember it. ‘das Schrecklichste’ is a superlative adjective used as a noun (das Schönste, das Beste). ‘bedächtig’ = slowly, thoughtfully. ‘austrinken’ = to finish (a drink). ‘strafen’ = to punish (die Strafe = punishment). ‘erbärmlich’ = pitiful, wretched.

units.covers: Chapters 'Auf der Suche nach den Idealen der Menschheit' (end) to 'Z und N'
units.en: The teacher admits that he does not believe in God. Back at camp, a boy called L reports that his camera has been stolen. At night the teacher and the sergeant hide by a haystack to check on the guards. Waiting in the moonlight, the teacher thinks about the Roman captain in the picture, who recognised God at the cross and still did nothing. At about two o'clock he sees Z, on guard, being handed a letter by a strange boy, who then disappears. Next day the teacher learns that Z and N fight all the time, because Z writes a diary at night and keeps it locked in a little box. The teacher decides: he must read that diary. In the afternoon, when everyone has marched off, he goes into their tent. A letter from N's mother lies on one sleeping bag.

Im Schlafsack nebenan war nichts versteckt. Hier schlief also der R. Dann muss das Kästchen im dritten liegen.
Dort lag es auch.
Es war ein Kästchen aus blauem Blech und hatte ein einfaches Schloss.
Es war versperrt. Ich versuchte, das Schloss mit einem Draht zu öffnen.
Es ließ sich leicht.
In dem Kästchen lagen Briefe, Postkarten und ein grüngebundenes Buch – „Mein Tagebuch“, stand da in goldenen Lettern.
units.en: There was nothing hidden in the sleeping bag next to it. So this was where R slept. Then the box had to be in the third one. And there it was. It was a box made of blue tin with a simple lock. It was locked. I tried to open the lock with a piece of wire. It opened easily. In the box were letters, postcards and a green-bound book – “My Diary”, it said in gold letters.
units.explain_en: The teacher is doing something wrong here – reading a pupil's private diary. ‘verstecken’ = to hide. ‘das Blech’ = tin, sheet metal. ‘versperrt’ is Austrian/southern German for ‘abgeschlossen’ (locked). ‘der Draht’ = wire. ‘Es ließ sich leicht’ (öffnen) = it could be opened easily – ‘sich lassen’ + infinitive means ‘can be done’: ‘Das lässt sich machen.’

Ich öffnete es.
„Weihnachten von Deiner Mutter.“
Wer war die Mutter des Z? Mir scheint, eine Beamtenwitwe oder so.
Dann kamen die ersten Eintragungen, etwas von einem Christbaum – ich blätterte weiter, wir sind schon nach Ostern. Zuerst hat er jeden Tag geschrieben, dann nur jeden zweiten, dritten, dann jeden fünften, sechsten und hier, hier liegt der Brief!
Er ist es! Ein zerknülltes Kuvert, ohne Aufschrift, ohne Marke!
Rasch! Was steht nur drin?!
„Kann heute nicht kommen, komme morgen um zwei – Eva.“
Das war alles.
Wer ist Eva?
Ich weiß nur, wer Adam ist.
Adam ist der Z.
Und ich lese das Tagebuch:
units.en: I opened it. “For Christmas, from your mother.” Who was Z's mother? A civil servant's widow or something like that, I think. Then came the first entries, something about a Christmas tree – I leafed on; we're already past Easter. At first he wrote every day, then only every second or third day, then every fifth or sixth, and here – here is the letter! That's it! A crumpled envelope, with no address, no stamp! Quick! What does it say?! “Can't come today, coming tomorrow at two – Eva.” That was all. Who is Eva? I only know who Adam is. Adam is Z. And I read the diary:
units.explain_en: The chapter is called ‘Adam und Eva’: Z and his secret girlfriend are like the first couple in the Garden of Eden. ‘die Eintragung’ = entry. ‘blättern’ = to leaf through pages. ‘zerknüllt’ = crumpled. ‘das Kuvert’ is Austrian for ‘der Briefumschlag’ (envelope). ‘die Marke’ here = ‘die Briefmarke’ (stamp). ‘Was steht drin?’ = What does it say?

units.en: The diary tells the teacher everything. During an exercise, Z got lost in the woods near some caves and met a girl with two barefoot boys – the robber children. The girl is an orphan. She ran away from a reform school (Besserungsanstalt) and now lives in a cave with a gang of village boys, stealing whatever she can; she is their leader. She and Z fell in love, and since then she has secretly visited him at night while he stands guard. He knows she stole L's camera, but he swears to protect her and never to let her go back to the reform school. The last lines are about N, who keeps threatening to smash the box: “Anyone who touches my box dies!”

units.de:
„Jeder, der mein Kästchen anrührt, stirbt!“
Ich lese den Satz zweimal und muss lächeln.
Kinderei!
Und ich will an das denken, was ich las, aber ich komme nicht dazu. Vom Waldrand her tönt die Trompete, ich muss mich beeilen, das Regiment naht. Rasch tu ich das Tagebuch wieder ins Kästchen und will es versperren. Ich drehe den Draht hin und her. Umsonst! Es lässt sich nicht mehr schließen, ich hab das Schloss verdorben – was tun?
Sie werden gleich da sein, die Jungen. Ich verstecke das offene Kästchen im Schlafsack und verlasse das Zelt. Es blieb mir nichts anderes übrig. Jetzt kommt das Regiment daher.
In der vierten Reihe marschiert der Z.
units.en: “Anyone who touches my box dies!” I read the sentence twice and have to smile. Childishness! And I want to think about what I have read, but I don't get the chance. A trumpet sounds from the edge of the wood; I have to hurry, the regiment is coming. Quickly I put the diary back into the box and try to lock it. I twist the wire this way and that. No use! It won't close any more; I've broken the lock – what now? They'll be here any moment, the boys. I hide the open box in the sleeping bag and leave the tent. There was nothing else I could do. Now the regiment comes marching along. Z is marching in the fourth row.
units.explain_en: This chapter is called ‘Verurteilt’ (Condemned). ‘die Kinderei’ = childishness. ‘Ich komme nicht dazu’ = I don't get round to it – very common. ‘sich beeilen’ = to hurry. ‘Umsonst!’ = in vain. ‘verderben’ (verdarb, verdorben) = to ruin; today you would say ‘kaputt machen’. ‘Es blieb mir nichts anderes übrig’ = I had no other choice – very useful. The boys are jokingly called ‘das Regiment’.

units.en: The teacher smiles again at this childishness – but then he stops smiling. In his mind he sees a prosecutor: Z has covered up a theft and could be arrested; he would be thrown out of school and the girl would go back to the reform school. Should the teacher tell the sergeant and the police, or first speak to Z alone? He watches Z asking what there is for dinner.

units.de:
Es sind schon größere Herren über die Liebe gestolpert, über die Liebe, die auch naturnotwendig ist und also ebenfalls gottgewollt. Und ich höre wieder den Pfaffen: „Das Schrecklichste auf der Welt ist Gott.“ Und ich höre einen wüsten Lärm, Geschrei und Gepolter. Alles stürzt zu einem Zelt.
Es ist das Zelt mit dem Kästchen. Der Z und der N raufen, man kann sie kaum trennen.
Der N ist rot, er blutet aus dem Mund.
Der Z ist weiß.
„Der N hat sein Kästchen erbrochen!“ ruft mir der Feldwebel zu.
units.en: Greater men than him have tripped over love – over love, which is also a necessity of nature and therefore also willed by God. And again I hear the priest: “The most terrible thing in the world is God.” And I hear a wild din, shouting and crashing. Everyone rushes to one of the tents. It is the tent with the box. Z and N are fighting; they can hardly be pulled apart. N is red; his mouth is bleeding. Z is white. “N broke his box open!” the sergeant calls to me.
units.explain_en: ‘Herren’ here means important men. ‘stolpern über’ = to trip over. ‘der Pfaffe’ is a disrespectful word for a priest – the teacher is angry. ‘wüst’ = wild, chaotic. ‘raufen’ = to fight, scuffle (southern German; also ‘sich prügeln’). ‘trennen’ = to separate. ‘bluten’ = to bleed. ‘erbrechen’ here is old for ‘aufbrechen’ (to break open). N is blamed for what the teacher did.

„Wer denn sonst?!“ schreit der Z. „Sagen Sies selber, Herr Lehrer, wer könnt es denn sonst schon getan haben?!“
„Lüge, Lüge!“

units.en: “No!” N shouts. “I didn't do it, not me!” “Who else, then?!” Z shouts. “You tell me, sir – who else could possibly have done it?!” “Lies, lies!” “He broke it open and nobody else! He already threatened he'd smash it!” “But I didn't do it!” “Quiet!” the sergeant suddenly roars. It is quiet. Z doesn't take his eyes off N. Anyone who touches his box dies – the thought suddenly goes through my head.
units.explain_en: ‘Ich habs nicht getan’ = ‘Ich habe es nicht getan’. ‘Herr Lehrer’ is how pupils addressed a teacher, like ‘sir’; today German pupils say ‘Herr/Frau’ + surname. ‘androhen’ = to threaten. ‘zertrümmern’ = to smash. ‘brüllen’ = to roar. ‘jemanden nicht aus den Augen lassen’ = not to take your eyes off someone. ‘Es geht mir durch den Sinn’ = it crosses my mind.

Unwillkürlich blick ich empor.
 Aber der Himmel ist sanft.
Ich fühle, der Z könnte den N umbringen.
Auch der N scheint es zu spüren. Er wendet sich kleinlaut an mich.
„Herr Lehrer, ich möcht in einem anderen Zelt schlafen.“
„Gut.“
„Ich habs wirklich nicht gelesen, sein Tagebuch. Helfen Sie mir, Herr Lehrer!“
„Ich werde dir helfen.“ Jetzt sieht mich der Z an. Du kannst nicht helfen, liegt in seinem Blick.
units.en: Without meaning to, I look up. But the sky is gentle. I feel that Z could kill N. N seems to sense it too. He turns to me meekly. “Sir, I'd like to sleep in a different tent.” “All right.” “I really didn't read it, his diary. Help me, sir!” “I'll help you.” Now Z looks at me. You can't help, his look says.
units.explain_en: ‘unwillkürlich’ = involuntarily, without meaning to. ‘sanft’ = gentle. ‘umbringen’ = to kill (informal). ‘spüren’ = to sense, feel. ‘kleinlaut’ = meek, subdued. ‘sich wenden an’ = to turn to (someone). ‘Ich möcht’ = ‘ich möchte’. Painful irony: the teacher promises to help N, but he is the one who could clear N – and he stays silent.

units.en: The teacher knows that by keeping quiet he has condemned N. Why doesn't he say that he opened the box? He is ashamed to admit it in front of everyone. He decides to tell Z privately, man to man, and that same night to talk to the girl too: she must stay away, and he will give Z a good talking-to. That should be the end of it.

Und ich werde den Z begnadigen. Und auch das Mädel. Ich lasse mich nicht unschuldig verurteilen! Ja, Gott ist schrecklich, aber ich will ihm einen Strich durch die Rechnung machen. Mit meinem freien Willen.
Einen dicken Strich.
Ich werde uns alle retten.
units.en: Guilt circles like a bird of prey. It seizes us quickly. But I will acquit N. After all, he hasn't done anything. And I will pardon Z. And the girl too. I won't let myself be condemned when I'm innocent! Yes, God is terrible, but I'm going to spoil His plans. With my free will. A thick line through His sums. I will save us all.

units.en: The teacher notices T staring at him with his pale fish eyes, smiling mockingly, just as at the funeral. Does T know something? That night the teacher hides in the woods near Z's guard post. At half past two Eva appears. The teacher watches the two of them together instead of stepping forward to confess. Clouds cover the moon; in the pitch dark his outstretched hand touches a face – someone is standing right beside him. Terrified, he waits for dawn, creeps back to his tent and oversleeps. The boys go out on an exercise and come back at lunchtime without N, who seems to be lost. Z, whose hands are scratched and whose jacket is torn, calmly tells the teacher that N confessed to breaking the box and that he forgave him. The teacher knows this is a lie.

units.de: Warum sagte ich es ihm nur nicht sofort, gleich gestern, als er den N verprügelte! Weil ich mich schämte, vor meinen Herren Schülern zu gestehen, dass ich heimlich mit einem Draht ein Kästchen erbrochen hab, obwohl dies in bester Absicht geschehen ist – verständlich, verständlich! Aber warum verschlief ich nur heute früh?! Richtig, ich saß ja in der Nacht im Wald und machte das Maul nicht auf! Und jetzt, jetzt dürfte es wenig nützen, wenn ich es aufmachen würde. Es ist zu spät.
units.en: Why didn't I tell him straight away, yesterday, when he beat N up! Because I was ashamed to confess in front of my gentlemen pupils that I had secretly broken open a box with a piece of wire, even though I did it with the best intentions – understandable, understandable! But why did I have to oversleep this morning?! Of course – I was sitting in the woods at night and kept my mouth shut! And now, now it probably wouldn't do much good if I opened it. It's too late.
units.explain_en: ‘verprügeln’ = to beat up. ‘gestehen’ = to confess. ‘in bester Absicht’ = with the best intentions. ‘heute früh’ is southern German for ‘heute Morgen’. ‘das Maul’ is an animal's mouth; ‘das Maul nicht aufmachen’ is rude/colloquial for ‘nichts sagen’ (today also ‘die Klappe halten’). ‘Es dürfte wenig nützen’ = it probably won't help much – ‘dürfte’ expresses probability.

units.en: The teacher feels that he is to blame too – he is the stone N tripped over. In the afternoon everyone searches the woods in the pouring rain, calling “N!”, but there is no answer. The sergeant wants to report N missing to the police, but the teacher says: tomorrow. “In that area there are no farms, only caves,” the sergeant says. The teacher remembers the caves in Z's diary.

units.de:
Am letzten Tage unseres Lagerlebens kam Gott.
Ich erwartete ihn bereits.
Der Feldwebel und die Jungen zerlegten gerade die Zelte, als er kam.
Sein Erscheinen war furchtbar. Dem Feldwebel wurde es übel, und er musste sich setzen. Die Jungen standen entsetzt herum, halb gelähmt. Erst allmählich bewegten sie sich wieder, und zwar immer aufgeregter.
Nur der Z bewegte sich kaum.
Er starrte zu Boden und ging auf und ab. Doch nur ein paar Meter. Immer hin und her.
Dann schrie alles durcheinander, so schien es mir.
Nur der Z blieb stumm.
Was war geschehen?
units.en: On the last day of our camp life, God came. I was already expecting Him. The sergeant and the boys were just taking down the tents when He came. His appearance was terrible. The sergeant felt sick and had to sit down. The boys stood around horrified, half paralysed. Only gradually did they start moving again, more and more agitatedly. Only Z hardly moved. He stared at the ground and walked up and down. But only a few metres. Back and forth, back and forth. Then everyone was shouting at once, or so it seemed to me. Only Z said nothing. What had happened?
units.explain_en: For the teacher, God now appears as the terrible truth coming to light. ‘das Lagerleben’ = camp life. ‘erwarten’ = to expect, wait for. ‘das Erscheinen’ = appearance. ‘Mir wird übel’ = I feel sick – very useful. ‘entsetzt’ = horrified. ‘gelähmt’ = paralysed. ‘allmählich’ = gradually. ‘stumm’ = silent, mute.

Zwei Waldarbeiter waren im Lager erschienen, zwei Holzfäller mit Rucksack, Säge und Axt. Sie berichteten, dass sie einen Jungen gefunden hätten. Sie hatten seinen Schulausweis bei sich.
Es war der N.
Er lag in der Nähe der Höhlen in einem Graben, unweit der Lichtung. Mit einer klaffenden Kopfwunde. Ein Stein musste ihn getroffen haben oder ein Schlag mit irgendeinem stumpfen Gegenstande.
Auf alle Fälle war er hin. Tot und tot.
units.en: Two forestry workers had turned up at the camp, two woodcutters with rucksacks, a saw and an axe. They reported that they had found a boy. They had his school pass with them. It was N. He was lying in a ditch near the caves, not far from the clearing. With a gaping head wound. A stone must have hit him, or a blow from some blunt object. In any case he was gone. Dead and dead.
units.explain_en: This is the turning point of the novel: N has been killed. ‘der Holzfäller’ = woodcutter. ‘berichten’ = to report. ‘der Ausweis’ = ID card, pass. ‘der Graben’ = ditch. ‘die Lichtung’ = clearing. ‘stumpf’ = blunt. ‘auf alle Fälle’ = in any case. ‘hin sein’ is colloquial for ‘kaputt’ or ‘tot’. ‘Tot und tot’ stresses how final it is.

units.en: The teacher goes down to the village police, and a murder squad arrives. N was hit from behind with a pointed stone about twenty metres from the ditch and then dragged into it. Near the body the police find the stone, a pencil and a compass. N's jacket is torn and his hands are scratched, as if there had been a fight. The teacher notices that Z's jacket is torn too and his hands are scratched – but he says nothing. The prosecutor questions everyone. When he asks the teacher whether he suspects anyone, the teacher says no. Then little R, who shared a tent with Z and N, pushes forward.

units.de:
„Herr Staatsanwalt“, schreit plötzlich der R und drängt sich vor, „der Z und der N haben sich immer gerauft! Der N hat nämlich das Tagebuch des Z gelesen, und deshalb war ihm der Z todfeind – er führt nämlich ein Tagebuch, es liegt in einem Kästchen aus blauem Blech!“ Alle blicken auf den Z.
Der steht mit gesenktem Haupt. Man kann sein Gesicht nicht sehen. Ist es weiß oder rot? Langsam tritt er vor. Er hält vor dem Staatsanwalt.
Es wird sehr still.
„Ja“, sagt er leise, „ich habs getan.“
Er weint.
Ich werfe einen Blick auf Gott.
Er lächelt.
Warum?
Und wie ich mich so frage, sehe ich ihn nicht mehr.
Er ist wieder fort.
units.en: “Mr Prosecutor,” R suddenly shouts, pushing forward, “Z and N were always fighting! You see, N read Z's diary, and that's why Z hated him like death – he keeps a diary, you see, it's in a little box made of blue tin!” Everyone looks at Z. He stands with his head bowed. You can't see his face. Is it white or red? Slowly he steps forward. He stops in front of the prosecutor. It becomes very quiet. “Yes,” he says quietly, “I did it.” He weeps. I glance at God. He smiles. Why? And as I ask myself that, I can no longer see Him. He has gone again.

units.en: It is autumn, and the trial is about to start. The newspapers are full of it. A reporter has twisted the teacher's words into praise of today's “dutiful” youth, and N's father, the baker, blames the teacher. Z's defence lawyer believes Z is covering for someone: the girl, Eva, who was arrested in her cave with her gang soon after the murder. The courtroom is packed. Z sits in the dock as if it were a school desk; his mother wears a thick black veil. The kindly old judge asks Z to tell his life story: Z wanted to become an inventor, or else a pilot flying mail overseas.

units.de:
Und wie der Z so von seiner ehemaligen Zukunft spricht, rückt die Zeit immer näher und näher – bald wird er da sein, der Tag, an dem der liebe Gott kam.
Der Z schildert das Lagerleben, das Schießen, Marschieren, das Hissen der Flagge, den Feldwebel und mich. Und er sagt einen sonderbaren Satz: „Die Ansichten des Herrn Lehrers waren mir oft zu jung.“
Der Präsident staunt.
„Wieso?“
„Weil der Herr Lehrer immer nur sagte, wie es auf der Welt sein sollte, und nie, wie es wirklich ist.“
units.en: And as Z talks like this about his former future, time moves closer and closer – soon it will be here, the day on which the good Lord came. Z describes life in the camp, the shooting, the marching, the raising of the flag, the sergeant and me. And he says a strange sentence: “I often found the teacher's views too young.” The judge is astonished. “Why?” “Because the teacher only ever said how things should be in the world, and never how they really are.”
units.explain_en: ‘seine ehemalige Zukunft’ (his former future) is a bitter phrase: his future is already lost. ‘schildern’ = to describe. ‘das Hissen der Flagge’ = raising the flag. ‘sonderbar’ = strange. ‘die Ansicht’ = view, opinion (‘meiner Ansicht nach’ = in my opinion). ‘der Präsident’ is the presiding judge. ‘staunen’ = to be amazed. Z's sentence shows the ‘fish’ generation: they simply accept the brutal world as it is.

units.de:
Der Präsident sieht den Z groß an. Fühlt er, dass nun ein Gebiet betreten wurde, wo das Radio regiert? Wo die Sehnsucht nach der Moral zum alten Eisen geworfen wird, während man vor der Brutalität der Wirklichkeit im Staube liegt? Ja, er scheint es zu fühlen, denn er sucht nach einer günstigen Gelegenheit, um die Erde verlassen zu können. Plötzlich fragt er den Z: „Glaubst du an Gott?“
„Ja“, sagt der Z, ohne zu überlegen.
„Und kennst du das fünfte Gebot?“
„Ja.“
„Bereust du deine Tat?“
Es wird sehr still im Saal.
„Ja“, meint der Z, „ich bereue sie sehr.“
Sie klang aber unecht, die Reue.
units.en: The judge looks at Z wide-eyed. Does he feel that they have now entered territory where the radio rules? Where the longing for morality is thrown on the scrap heap while people lie in the dust before the brutality of reality? Yes, he seems to feel it, because he looks for a good opportunity to leave the earth. Suddenly he asks Z: “Do you believe in God?” “Yes,” says Z without thinking. “And do you know the fifth commandment?” “Yes.” “Do you regret what you did?” It becomes very quiet in the courtroom. “Yes,” says Z, “I regret it very much.” But the regret sounded false.
units.explain_en: ‘die Sehnsucht nach’ = longing for. ‘zum alten Eisen werfen’ = to throw on the scrap heap. ‘die Gelegenheit’ = opportunity. ‘die Erde verlassen’ – the judge wants to escape into religion. The fifth commandment (in Catholic and Lutheran counting) is ‘Du sollst nicht töten’ – Thou shalt not kill. ‘bereuen’ = to regret (die Reue = remorse). ‘unecht’ = fake, not genuine.

units.en: Z says he met N on a rock, they fought, and he threw the stone – but he can't remember where. The judge assumes that the compass found by the body is Z's, and Z says he simply forgot, but the defence lawyer suggests it belonged to a third person. Z insists there wasn't and begs his lawyer to stop defending him. During the lunch break the teacher sees Z's mother sitting alone on a bench. He now believes in God, but he doesn't like Him. He goes to buy cigarettes in a tiny shop run by a very old, kind couple. While the old woman goes out to get change, the old man says that in this case everyone is guilty – even the parents, because they have forgotten God.

units.de: Ich sehe die hohen grauen Häuser und sage: „Wenn man nur wüsste, wo Gott wohnt.“ „Er wohnt überall, wo er nicht vergessen wurde“, höre ich die Stimme des Alten. „Er wohnt auch hier bei uns, denn wir streiten uns nie.“ Ich halte den Atem an. Was war das? War das noch die Stimme des Alten? Nein, das war nicht seine – das war eine andere Stimme. Wer sprach da zu mir? Ich dreh mich nicht um.
units.en: I look at the tall grey houses and say: “If only one knew where God lives.” “He lives wherever He hasn't been forgotten,” I hear the old man's voice say. “He lives here with us too, because we never quarrel.” I hold my breath. What was that? Was that still the old man's voice? No, it wasn't his – it was a different voice. Who was speaking to me? I don't turn round.
units.explain_en: ‘Wenn man nur wüsste …’ = If only one knew … (Konjunktiv II for a wish). ‘wo er nicht vergessen wurde’ is passive: where He hasn't been forgotten. ‘sich streiten’ = to quarrel, argue – very common. ‘den Atem anhalten’ = to hold one's breath. ‘sich umdrehen’ = to turn round; ‘dreh’ is short for ‘drehe’.

Da werd ich doch nur bestraft, weil ich den Dieb nicht verhaften ließ! „Das sollst du auch!“ Aber ich verliere auch meine Stellung, mein Brot – „Du musst es verlieren, damit kein neues Unrecht entsteht.“ Und meine Eltern?! Ich unterstütze sie ja! „Soll ich dir deine Kindheit zeigen?“ Meine Kindheit?
units.en: And again I hear the voice: “When you give evidence as a witness and speak my name, do not keep silent about the fact that you broke open the box.” The box! No! Then I'll only be punished for not having the thief arrested! “So you shall be!” But I'll lose my job too, my bread – “You must lose it, so that no new injustice arises.” And my parents?! I support them! “Shall I show you your childhood?” My childhood?

Ich möchte weinen.

units.en: My mother nags, my father rants. They are always quarrelling. No, You don't live here. Here You only pass by, and Your coming brings no joy – I feel like crying. “Say it,” I hear the voice, “say that you broke open the box. Do me this favour and do not hurt me again.”

units.en: The witnesses are heard. The baker attacks the teacher's opinions. Z's mother declares that the compass isn't her son's and that whoever lost it is the murderer. Z says his mother is lying and bursts out that she never cared about him and once treated a fifteen-year-old maid, Thekla, so badly that the girl stole money to run away and was sent to a reform school – a girl just like Eva. Then it is the teacher's turn. He swears before God to tell the whole truth and hide nothing. While he is being sworn in, Eva is led into the courtroom behind him.

units.de: Ich beantworte die Fragen des Präsidenten. Er streift auch wieder die Neger – ja, wir verstehen uns. Ich stelle dem N ein gutes Zeugnis aus und ebenso dem Z. Beim Mord war ich nicht dabei. Der Präsident will mich schon entlassen, da falle ich ihm ins Wort: „Nur noch eine Kleinigkeit, Herr Präsident!“ „Bitte!“ „Jenes Kästchen, in welchem das Tagebuch des Z lag, erbrach nicht der N.“ „Nicht der N? Sondern?“ „Sondern ich. Ich war es, der das Kästchen mit einem Draht öffnete.“
units.en: I answer the judge's questions. He touches on the Negroes again – yes, we understand each other. I give N a good report, and Z too. I wasn't there when the murder happened. The judge is about to dismiss me when I interrupt him: “Just one more small thing, Your Honour!” “Go ahead!” “That box in which Z's diary lay was not broken open by N.” “Not by N? Then by whom?” “By me. I was the one who opened the box with a piece of wire.”
units.explain_en: This is the teacher's great moment of courage. ‘streifen’ = to touch on (a subject). ‘jemandem ein gutes Zeugnis ausstellen’ = to speak well of someone (das Zeugnis = school report). ‘entlassen’ = to dismiss, release. ‘jemandem ins Wort fallen’ = to interrupt someone. ‘Bitte!’ here = go ahead. ‘Sondern?’ = but who, then? Remember: ‘Neger’ is a racist slur today – say ‘Schwarze Menschen’.

units.de:
Die Wirkung dieser Worte war groß.
Der Präsident ließ den Bleistift fallen, der Verteidiger schnellte empor, der Z glotzte mich an mit offenem Munde, seine Mutter schrie auf, der Bäckermeister wurde bleich wie Teig und griff sich ans Herz.
Und Eva?
Ich weiß es nicht.
Ich fühle nur eine allgemeine ängstliche Unruhe hinter mir.
Es murrt, es tuschelt.
Der Staatsanwalt erhebt sich hypnotisiert und deutet langsam mit dem Finger nach mir. „Sie?!“ fragt er gedehnt.
„Ja“, sage ich und wundere mich über meine Ruhe.
Ich fühle mich wunderbar leicht.
Und erzähle nun alles.
units.en: These words had a great effect. The judge dropped his pencil, the defence lawyer shot up, Z gaped at me open-mouthed, his mother cried out, the baker went as pale as dough and clutched his heart. And Eva? I don't know. I only feel a general anxious unrest behind me. There is muttering, whispering. The prosecutor rises as if hypnotised and slowly points his finger at me. “You?!” he asks, drawing the word out. “Yes,” I say, and I'm surprised at how calm I am. I feel wonderfully light. And now I tell everything.
units.explain_en: ‘die Wirkung’ = effect. ‘der Verteidiger’ = defence lawyer. ‘emporschnellen’ = to shoot up. ‘glotzen’ = to gape (rude). ‘bleich wie Teig’ = pale as dough – a joke about the baker. ‘sich ans Herz greifen’ = to clutch one's heart. ‘tuscheln’ = to whisper. ‘gedehnt’ = drawn out. ‘die Ruhe’ = calm. Telling the truth makes him feel ‘wunderbar leicht’.

units.de:
Warum ich das Kästchen erbrach und weshalb ich es dem Z nicht sogleich gestand. Weil ich mich nämlich schämte, aber es war auch eine Feigheit dabei.
Ich erzähle alles.
Weshalb ich das Tagebuch las und warum ich keine gesetzlichen Konsequenzen zog, denn ich wollte einen Strich durch eine Rechnung ziehen. Einen dicken Strich. Durch eine andere Rechnung. Ja, ich war dumm! Ich bemerke, dass der Staatsanwalt zu notieren beginnt, aber das stört mich nicht.
Alles, alles!
Erzähl nur zu!
Auch Adam und Eva. Und die finsteren Wolken und den Mann im Mond!
units.en: Why I broke open the box and why I didn't admit it to Z straight away. Because I was ashamed, you see – but there was cowardice in it too. I tell everything. Why I read the diary and why I didn't take any legal steps: because I wanted to draw a line through a sum. A thick line. Through a different sum. Yes, I was stupid! I notice that the prosecutor is starting to take notes, but that doesn't bother me. Everything, everything! Go on, tell it all! Adam and Eve too. And the dark clouds and the man in the moon!
units.explain_en: The sentences without a main verb continue ‘Und erzähle nun alles’: (I tell) why …, why …. ‘gestehen’ = to admit. ‘die Feigheit’ = cowardice. ‘gesetzliche Konsequenzen ziehen’ = to take legal action. ‘notieren’ = to take notes. ‘Das stört mich nicht’ = that doesn't bother me – very useful. ‘Erzähl nur zu!’ = go on, keep telling!

units.en: When the teacher has finished, the prosecutor warns him that he may be charged with misleading the authorities and covering up a theft. N's father shouts that the teacher has his son's death on his conscience, then suffers a heart attack and has to be led out. N's mother raises her arm and cries: “Fear God!”

 Still wie die dunklen Seen in den Wäldern meiner Heimat. Eva, bist du schon der Herbst?

units.covers: Chapters 'Vertrieben aus dem Paradies' and 'Der Fisch' (beginning)
units.en: Eva is questioned. She says she wants to tell the truth, like the teacher. She was there: N and Z fought, N threw Z down from the rock, and she, furious, picked up a stone and ran after N. But a strange boy jumped out of the bushes, grabbed the stone, caught up with N, struck him from behind and dragged him into the ditch. Z took the blame because he believed Eva had done it. The prosecutor mocks the “great unknown”. Then Eva says quietly that she never loved Z. Asked whether she would recognise the strange boy, she answers:

units.de: „Vielleicht. Ich erinner mich nur, er hatte helle, runde Augen. Wie ein Fisch.“ Das Wort versetzt mir einen Hieb. Ich springe auf und schreie: „Ein Fisch?!“ „Was ist Ihnen?“ fragt der Präsident und wundert sich. Alles staunt. Ja, was ist mir denn nur? Ich denke an einen illuminierten Totenkopf. Es kommen kalte Zeiten, höre ich Julius Caesar, das Zeitalter der Fische. Da wird die Seele des Menschen unbeweglich wie das Antlitz eines Fisches. Zwei helle, runde Augen sehen mich an. Ohne Schimmer, ohne Glanz. Es ist der T.
units.en: “Maybe. I only remember he had pale, round eyes. Like a fish.” The word hits me like a blow. I jump up and shout: “A fish?!” “What's the matter with you?” asks the judge in surprise. Everyone is astonished. Yes, what is the matter with me? I think of a skull that lights up. Cold times are coming, I hear Julius Caesar say, the Age of the Fish. Then the human soul will become as motionless as the face of a fish. Two pale, round eyes are looking at me. Without a gleam, without a shine. It is T.
units.explain_en: Everything comes together: the ‘fish’ is T. ‘Ich erinner mich’ = ‘Ich erinnere mich’ (sich erinnern an = to remember). ‘der Hieb’ = blow. ‘Was ist Ihnen?’ is old-fashioned for ‘Was ist mit Ihnen los?’ ‘illuminiert’ = lit up – Julius Caesar's skull tie-pin. The repeated phrases from earlier chapters (‘Ohne Schimmer, ohne Glanz’) show the teacher's memory racing.

units.de: Und wieder fragt der Präsident: „Was ist Ihnen?“ Soll ich es sagen, dass ich an den T denke? Unsinn! Warum sollte denn der T den N erschlagen haben? Es fehlt doch jedes Motiv – Und ich sage: „Verzeihung, Herr Präsident, aber ich bin etwas nervös.“ „Begreiflich!“ grinst der Staatsanwalt. Ich verlasse den Saal. Ich weiß, sie werden den Z freisprechen und das Mädel verurteilen. Aber ich weiß auch, es wird sich alles ordnen. Morgen oder übermorgen wird die Untersuchung gegen mich eingeleitet werden. Wegen Irreführung der Behörde und Diebstahlsbegünstigung. Man wird mich vom Lehramt suspendieren. Ich verliere mein Brot.
units.en: And again the judge asks: “What's the matter with you?” Should I say that I'm thinking of T? Nonsense! Why would T have killed N? There's no motive at all – And I say: “I beg your pardon, Your Honour, but I'm a little nervous.” “Understandable!” grins the prosecutor. I leave the courtroom. I know they will acquit Z and convict the girl. But I also know that everything will be put right. Tomorrow or the day after, an investigation will be opened against me. For misleading the authorities and covering up a theft. They'll suspend me from teaching. I'll lose my bread.
units.explain_en: ‘Unsinn!’ = nonsense. ‘das Motiv’ = motive. ‘Verzeihung’ = excuse me, sorry. ‘begreiflich’ = understandable (today: ‘verständlich’). ‘freisprechen’ = to acquit; ‘verurteilen’ = to convict. ‘sich ordnen’ = to sort itself out. ‘übermorgen’ = the day after tomorrow – useful! ‘die Untersuchung’ = investigation. ‘suspendieren’ = to suspend.

units.en: The teacher goes home to bed, strangely free of worries. Next morning the paper reports that Z got only a small sentence, while Eva has been charged with murder. The teacher is banned from the school. He waits for T after school and buys him an ice cream. T calmly says Eva made up the strange boy, reveals that he watched the teacher that night in the woods – it was his face the teacher touched – and claims the pupils call the teacher “the Fish”. Then T stops, as if he has said too much. The next day is a state holiday for the dictator's birthday, full of flags and marching. A quiet boy, B, visits the teacher: the compass belonged to T, and T once said he would like to watch someone die. B has skipped the parade; he hates the marching and the speeches.
